claim: Memory impairment in chronic pain patients is substantial and common.
source: Memory impairment in chronic pain patients is substantial and common, and few therapeutic strategies are available.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature establishing the prevalence and significance of memory impairment in chronic pain patients.

claim: Few therapeutic strategies are available for chronic pain-related memory impairment.
source: Memory impairment in chronic pain patients is substantial and common, and few therapeutic strategies are available.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of therapeutic options, supported by the context of the research need.

claim: Chronic pain-related memory impairment has susceptible and unsusceptible features.
source: Chronic pain-related memory impairment has susceptible and unsusceptible features.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing segregation of mice into susceptible and unsusceptible subpopulations.

claim: Chronic pain mice were segregated into memory impairment-susceptible and -unsusceptible subpopulations using Y-maze test and Morris water maze.
source: combining two spatial memory tests (Y-maze test and Morris water maze), we segregated chronic pain mice into memory impairment-susceptible and -unsusceptible subpopulations in a chronic neuropathic pain model induced by chronic constrictive injury of the sciatic nerve.
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental methods and results described in the manuscript.

claim: S1P/S1PR1 signaling is a determinant for vulnerability to chronic pain-related memory impairment.
source: RNA-Seq analysis and gain/loss-of-function study revealed that S1P/S1PR1 signaling is a determinant for vulnerability to chronic pain-related memory impairment.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data and functional experiments involving knockdown and overexpression of S1PR1.

claim: Knockdown of S1PR1 in the dentate gyrus promoted a susceptible phenotype.
source: Knockdown of the S1PR1 in the dentate gyrus (DG) promoted a susceptible phenotype and led to structural plasticity changes of reduced excitatory synapse formation and abnormal spine morphology as observed in susceptible mice
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from viral knockdown experiments and behavioral testing.

claim: Knockdown of S1PR1 in the dentate gyrus led to reduced excitatory synapse formation.
source: Knockdown of the S1PR1 in the dentate gyrus (DG) promoted a susceptible phenotype and led to structural plasticity changes of reduced excitatory synapse formation and abnormal spine morphology as observed in susceptible mice
evidence: This is supported by TEM and Golgi staining data showing structural changes.

claim: Knockdown of S1PR1 in the dentate gyrus led to abnormal spine morphology.
source: Knockdown of the S1PR1 in the dentate gyrus (DG) promoted a susceptible phenotype and led to structural plasticity changes of reduced excitatory synapse formation and abnormal spine morphology as observed in susceptible mice
evidence: This is supported by Golgi staining data showing changes in dendritic spine morphology.

claim: Overexpression of S1PR1 in the dentate gyrus promoted an unsusceptible phenotype.
source: while overexpression of the S1PR1 and pharmacological administration of S1PR1 agonist in the DG promoted an unsusceptible phenotype and prevented the occurrence of memory impairment, and rescued the morphological abnormality.
evidence: This is supported by viral overexpression experiments and behavioral testing.

claim: Overexpression of S1PR1 in the dentate gyrus prevented the occurrence of memory impairment.
source: while overexpression of the S1PR1 and pharmacological administration of S1PR1 agonist in the DG promoted an unsusceptible phenotype and prevented the occurrence of memory impairment, and rescued the morphological abnormality.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from Y-maze and MWM tests.

claim: Pharmacological administration of S1PR1 agonist in the dentate gyrus promoted an unsusceptible phenotype.
source: while overexpression of the S1PR1 and pharmacological administration of S1PR1 agonist in the DG promoted an unsusceptible phenotype and prevented the occurrence of memory impairment, and rescued the morphological abnormality.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological experiments using SEW2871 and behavioral testing.

claim: Pharmacological administration of S1PR1 agonist in the dentate gyrus rescued morphological abnormality.
source: while overexpression of the S1PR1 and pharmacological administration of S1PR1 agonist in the DG promoted an unsusceptible phenotype and prevented the occurrence of memory impairment, and rescued the morphological abnormality.
evidence: This is supported by TEM and Golgi staining data showing restoration of structural plasticity.

claim: Downregulation of S1PR1 in susceptible mice may impair DG structural plasticity via interaction with actin cytoskeleton rearrangement-related signaling pathways including Itga2 and its downstream Rac1/Cdc42 signaling and Arp2/3 cascade.
source: Finally, the Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis and biochemical evidence indicated that downregulation of S1PR1 in susceptible mice may impair DG structural plasticity via interaction with actin cytoskeleton rearrangement-related signaling pathways including Itga2 and its downstream Rac1/Cdc42 signaling and Arp2/3 cascade.
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis, western blot data, and co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Clinical and preclinical studies have demonstrated that chronic pain impairs memory or accelerates memory decline.
source: Clinical and preclinical studies have demonstrated that chronic pain impairs memory or accelerates memory decline (Whitlock et al., 2017; Phelps et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Memory impairment is a potential contributing factor to the maintenance of chronic pain and poor treatment response.
source: Memory impairment is also a potential contributing factor to the maintenance of chronic pain and poor treatment response (Phelps et al., 2021; Wiech, 2016; Moriarty et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Memory deficits in chronic pain patients exhibit high heterogeneity.
source: Although memory deficits in chronic pain patients are substantial and common, some clinical observations indicate high heterogeneity (Whitlock et al., 2017; Innes and Sambamoorthi, 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical observations.

claim: Few preclinical studies model the clinical scenario of susceptible and unsusceptible features of chronic pain-related memory impairment.
source: However, few preclinical studies model this clinical scenario and explore its underlying mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in the literature that this study addresses.

claim: Cognitive dysfunction associated with chronic pain is linked to structural and functional deficits within the hippocampus.
source: Findings from both human and animal studies have indicated that cognitive dysfunction associated with chronic pain is linked to structural and functional deficits within the hippocampus (Tajerian et al., 2018; Tajerian et al., 2014; Xia et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Mutso et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior human and animal studies.

claim: The dentate gyrus plays a crucial role in memory formation processing.
source: In particular, the dentate gyrus (DG), as part of the hippocampus, plays a crucial role in memory formation processing (Zhang et al., 2008; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on DG function.

claim: The DG performs pattern separation.
source: The DG has been postulated to perform a variety of mnemonic tasks, such as pattern separation (Gilbert et al., 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The DG performs novelty detection.
source: novelty detection (Hunsaker et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The DG processes information related to spatial contexts.
source: and processing information related to spatial contexts (Lee and Jung, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The impact of pain-related cognitive syndromes on the dendritic morphologies of DG neurons is inconsistent across different studies.
source: Nevertheless, the impact of pain-related cognitive syndromes on the dendritic morphologies of DG neurons, such as dendritic complexity, is inconsistent across different studies (Tajerian et al., 2018; Tajerian et al., 2014; Tyrtyshnaia and Manzhulo, 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations showing variability in prior findings.

claim: The molecular mechanisms of how pain-related cognitive syndromes affect DG neurons remain minimally understood.
source: and the molecular mechanisms remain minimally understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that this study addresses.

claim: The principal cell type of the DG is the dentate granule cells (DGCs).
source: The principal cell type of the DG is the dentate granule cells (DGCs), which are divided into immature and mature ones (Amaral et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on DG cell types.

claim: Immature newborn DGCs undergo neurogenesis and play key roles in learning and memory due to their high excitability and enhanced synaptic plasticity.
source: Immature newborn DGCs undergo neurogenesis and play key roles in learning and memory due to their high excitability and enhanced synaptic plasticity (Kempermann et al., 1997; Ninkovic et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on immature DGCs.

claim: Mice with chronic pain-related memory impairment showed significantly reduced adult neurogenesis in the DG.
source: Our previous study found that mice with chronic pain-related memory impairment showed significantly reduced adult neurogenesis in the DG (Xia et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Mature DGCs are less excitable and exhibit reduced synaptic plasticity.
source: Contrarily, mature DGCs are less excitable and exhibit reduced synaptic plasticity to an extent
evidence: This is a statement about the known properties of mature DGCs.

claim: Mature DGCs are equally recruited in memory formation.
source: but emerging evidence suggests that this cell population is equally recruited in memory formation (Tronel et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2012; Ramirez et al., 2013; Redondo et al., 2014; Ryan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: S1P is a bioactive sphingolipid metabolite.
source: Sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) is a bioactive sphingolipid metabolite, functioning as a key signaling molecule in a variety of cellular processes, such as cell division, adhesion, migration, and death (Spiegel et al., 1996; Spiegel and Milstien, 2003; Cui et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on S1P.

claim: S1P functions as a key signaling molecule in cell division, adhesion, migration, and death.
source: Sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) is a bioactive sphingolipid metabolite, functioning as a key signaling molecule in a variety of cellular processes, such as cell division, adhesion, migration, and death (Spiegel et al., 1996; Spiegel and Milstien, 2003; Cui et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on S1P functions.

claim: S1P acts through both extracellular and intracellular modes.
source: S1P acts both through extracellular and intracellular modes (Spiegel and Milstien, 2003; Cui et al., 2022; Maceyka et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on S1P signaling modes.

claim: The S1P system is a modulator of pain and memory processing pathways through S1P receptors 1–5 (S1PR1–5), particularly S1PR1.
source: In its extracellular mode, increasing evidence has suggested that the S1P system is a modulator of pain and memory processing pathways through S1P receptors 1–5 (S1PR1–5), particularly S1PR1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the context of prior literature on S1P receptors.

claim: Astrocyte-mediated S1PR1 neuroinflammation contributes to central sensitization through increased S1P production and IL-1β release in the spinal cord in models of traumatic nerve injury.
source: For instance, in models of traumatic nerve injury, astrocyte-mediated S1PR1 neuroinflammation contributes to central sensitization through increased S1P production and IL-1β release in the spinal cord, and beneficial effects of pain alleviation can be observed following IL-10-dependent S1PR1 antagonism (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Beneficial effects of pain alleviation can be observed following IL-10-dependent S1PR1 antagonism in models of traumatic nerve injury.
source: For instance, in models of traumatic nerve injury, astrocyte-mediated S1PR1 neuroinflammation contributes to central sensitization through increased S1P production and IL-1β release in the spinal cord, and beneficial effects of pain alleviation can be observed following IL-10-dependent S1PR1 antagonism (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The role of S1P signaling in higher pain centers remains largely unexplored.
source: While there is evidence on S1P signaling regulating pain perception in the spinal cord, its role in higher pain centers remains largely unexplored.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that this study addresses.

claim: CNS S1PR1 agonism may regulate the cellular repositioning of new DGCs and the integration of new neurons into pre-existing circuits, which may govern memory formation.
source: In regard to S1P function in memory processing, a recent study has hinted at the possibility of CNS S1PR1 agonism in the cellular repositioning of new DGCs and in regulating the integration of new neurons into pre-existing circuits, which may govern the process of memory formation (Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Activation of S1PR1 after traumatic brain injury in rats can significantly enhance neurogenesis and neurocognitive function.
source: Additionally, activation of S1PR1 after traumatic brain injury in rats can significantly enhance neurogenesis and neurocognitive function (Ye et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The S1P receptor signaling pathway has profound effects on the regulation of synaptic strength, including modulating synaptic architecture and plasticity, and mediating excitatory synaptic transmission in the hippocampus.
source: Importantly, increasing evidence suggests that the S1P receptor signaling pathway has profound effects on the regulation of synaptic strength, including modulating synaptic architecture and plasticity, and mediating excitatory synaptic transmission in the hippocampus (Kanno et al., 2010; Riganti et al., 2016; Mitroi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There is limited understanding regarding the involvement of S1P signaling in chronic pain-related memory impairment.
source: However, there is limited understanding regarding the involvement of S1P signaling in chronic pain-related memory impairment, as well as the interactive pathways that may underlie the effects.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that this study addresses.

claim: CCI induced long-lasting mechanical allodynia.
source: CCI-induced long-lasting mechanical allodynia (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CCI induced thermal hyperalgesia.
source: and thermal hyperalgesia (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No significant change in locomotor functions was observed in CCI mice.
source: No significant change in locomotor functions was observed in these injured mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Only chronic (21–28 days) and not acute (5–7 days) exposure to constrictive injury-induced neuropathic pain impaired spatial memory formation in both Y-maze test and Morris water maze test.
source: Consistent with our recent study (Xia et al., 2020), only chronic (21–28 days, referred to as CCI-Chronic) and not acute (5–7 days, referred to as CCI-Acute) exposure to constrictive injury-induced neuropathic pain impaired spatial memory formation in both Y-maze test (Figure 1A, B, D, E) and Morris water maze (MWM) test (Figure 1A, C, F, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1A-G and citation to prior work.

claim: A ratio of 40% (percent time spent in the novel arm) was set as the cutoff value for Y-maze test to segregate susceptible and unsusceptible mice.
source: Using this algorithm, a ratio of 40% (percent time spent in the novel arm) and a ratio of 36% (percent time in the target quadrant) were set as cutoff values for Y-maze test (Figure 1E, left) and MWM test (Figure 1G, left), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the k-means clustering algorithm analysis and data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A ratio of 36% (percent time in the target quadrant) was set as the cutoff value for MWM test to segregate susceptible and unsusceptible mice.
source: Using this algorithm, a ratio of 40% (percent time spent in the novel arm) and a ratio of 36% (percent time in the target quadrant) were set as cutoff values for Y-maze test (Figure 1E, left) and MWM test (Figure 1G, left), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the k-means clustering algorithm analysis and data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In the Y-maze test, 43% of CCI-Chronic mice were unsusceptible, and the remaining 57% were susceptible.
source: Accordingly, in the Y-maze test, 43% of CCI-Chronic mice were unsusceptible, and the remaining 57% were susceptible (Figure 1E, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In the MWM test, 52% of CCI-Chronic mice were unsusceptible, and 48% were susceptible.
source: In the MWM test, 52% of CCI-Chronic mice were unsusceptible, and 48% were susceptible (Figure 1G, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The majority of CCI-Chronic mice exhibited consistent memory performance in the Y-maze and MWM tests (susceptible: 47%; unsusceptible: 43%).
source: The bar graph (Figure 1H, right) showed that the majority of CCI-Chronic mice exhibited consistent memory performance in the two behavioral tests (susceptible: 47%; unsusceptible: 43%)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Only 10% of CCI-Chronic mice displayed susceptibility in a single test (Y-maze: 8%; MWM, 2%).
source: and only 10% of mice displayed susceptibility in a single test (Y-maze: 8%; MWM, 2%), suggesting good agreement between the two different assays.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Memory impairment can last at least 63 days post CCI surgery.
source: The results showed that memory impairment can last at least 63 days post CCI surgery, providing a workable time window for further investigations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: There is no correlation between memory performance and thermal pain threshold in CCI mice.
source: The statistics revealed no correlation between memory performance for each mouse against its thermal pain threshold (r2 = 0.04, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A; r2 = 0.05, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: Meloxicam analgesia could not relieve memory impairment in CCI-Chronic mice.
source: During the duration of analgesic effects (day 34–35 post CCI) (Figure 1I), we conducted the Y-maze test and found that the analgesia could not relieve the memory impairment (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1I and 1J.

claim: The percentage of susceptible and unsusceptible mice remained stable after meloxicam treatment.
source: Consistently, the percentage of susceptible and unsusceptible mice remained stable (Figure 1K), further indicating that the susceptibility or insusceptibility to memory impairment is marginally correlated with the pain tolerance of mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The susceptibility or insusceptibility to memory impairment is marginally correlated with the pain tolerance of mice.
source: Consistently, the percentage of susceptible and unsusceptible mice remained stable (Figure 1K), further indicating that the susceptibility or insusceptibility to memory impairment is marginally correlated with the pain tolerance of mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by the meloxicam experiment data and correlation analysis.

claim: A total of 510 differentially expressed genes were detected between Sham and susceptible mice, with 330 genes (65%) upregulated and 180 genes (35%) downregulated.
source: We detected a total of 510 differentially expressed genes between Sham and susceptible mice, with 330 genes (65%) upregulated and 180 genes (35%) downregulated (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: KEGG analysis revealed significant enrichment of six downregulated genes in the lipid metabolism pathway for Sham versus susceptible mice.
source: We noticed that Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analysis revealed significant enrichment of six downregulated genes in the lipid metabolism pathway for Sham versus susceptible mice (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG analysis data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Sphingolipid metabolism was significantly enriched in the trend pattern of Sham versus unsusceptible versus susceptible mice.
source: Combining the trend analysis of Sham versus unsusceptible versus susceptible mice, we found in the trend pattern of Figure 2D (left: Sham; middle, unsusceptible; right: susceptible), sphingolipid metabolism was significantly enriched (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by trend analysis data shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: Transcription of Sptlc3 was downregulated in susceptible mice.
source: In particular, transcription of Sptlc3 was downregulated (Figure 2C, E).

claim: Sptlc3 encodes the subunit of the serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) which catalyzes the rate-limiting step in sphingolipid biosynthesis.
source: Sptlc3 encodes the subunit of the serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) which catalyzes the rate-limiting step in sphingolipid biosynthesis (Hornemann et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on Sptlc3 function.

claim: Defective SPT leads to disturbed sphingolipid homeostasis and failure of the subsequent production of metabolites such as glucosylceramide and sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P).
source: Defective SPT leads to disturbed sphingolipid homeostasis and failure of the subsequent production of metabolites such as glucosylceramide (Zhang et al., 2011) and sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) (Gorshkova et al., 2012), contributing to the occurrence of biological disorders.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on SPT function.

claim: S1P/S1PR1 signaling is highly involved in hippocampus-engaged behaviors.
source: Previous studies have found that S1P/S1PR1 signaling is highly involved in hippocampus-engaged behaviors (Yang et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: No change of S1PR1 was observed on day 7 after CCI.

evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 2F and 2H.

claim: Significant downregulation of S1PR1 was observed in susceptible mice compared with Sham and unsusceptible ones.
source: but significant downregulation in susceptible mice compared with Sham and unsusceptible ones (Figure 2G, I).

claim: S1PR1 was mostly co-expressed with neuronal nuclear protein (NeuN) in neurons.
source: Immunofluorescence staining results showed that S1PR1 was mostly co-expressed with neuronal nuclear protein (NeuN) in neurons and merely co-expressed with glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) in astrocytes or ionized calcium-binding adaptor molecule 1 (Iba1) in microglia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, C.

claim: S1PR1 was merely co-expressed with GFAP in astrocytes or Iba1 in microglia.
source: Immunofluorescence staining results showed that S1PR1 was mostly co-expressed with neuronal nuclear protein (NeuN) in neurons and merely co-expressed with glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) in astrocytes or ionized calcium-binding adaptor molecule 1 (Iba1) in microglia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, C).

claim: S1PR1 was highly co-expressed with CaMKII-expressing excitatory neurons.

claim: S1PR1 was sparsely co-expressed with GAD67-expressing inhibitory neurons.

claim: Reduction of S1PR1 in the DG enhanced the memory impairment of CCI-treated mice in the Y-maze test.

claim: Overexpression of S1PR1 in CCI-treated mice significantly improved the spatial memory formation by promoting insusceptibility to memory impairment (up to 82%).

claim: Overexpression of S1PR1 in the DG had no obvious effects on Sham-treated mice in Y-maze and MWM tests.
